name: Sonic cleansing brush
lead: A sonic cleansing brush is a handheld, battery-powered device with a soft-bristled head that oscillates rapidly to cleanse the face. People use it with a liquid or gel cleanser to lift makeup, sebum and environmental particles from the skin, aiming for cleaner, clearer-looking skin and a better base for the rest of a skincare routine.[1][4]

Clarisonic is the brand most associated with the category. Pacific Bioscience Laboratories of Redmond, Washington, founded in 2001, launched the first Clarisonic sonic facial-cleansing brush in 2004; L'Oreal acquired the company in 2011 and announced in July 2020 that it would discontinue the brand.[4] Many other manufacturers now sell similar tools.

The published research is modest and mostly concerns cleansing: a literature review of facial cleansing with sonic brushes in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology,[1] a laboratory-style study that used an artificial sebum-and-particulate pollution model to compare a sonic brush with manual cleansing,[2] and a multi-center cohort study of a brush with an acne head and gel cleanser in people with mild-to-moderate acne.[3]

paras: The device consists of a handle containing a motor and a removable brush head. Heads are sold in different bristle types for general cleansing, sensitive skin or acne-prone skin, and some are designed for specific purposes such as the acne brush head used in one published cohort study [3]. Models differ in oscillation speed, number of settings and waterproofing.

The head moves at high frequency to loosen oil, makeup and particles from the skin surface so that cleanser can be rinsed away more effectively than with hands alone. A 2017 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science developed a model in which particulate matter is trapped in sebum-like oils on skin, to evaluate the cleansing efficacy of a sonic brush versus manual cleansing [2].

Pacific Bioscience Laboratories was founded in 2001 by David Giuliani, Robb Akridge, Steve Meginniss, Ward Harris and Ken Pilcher. Giuliani had previously co-founded Optiva, which developed the Sonicare toothbrush line, and Pilcher is described as the lead inventor of Clarisonic's skin care systems.[4] The first Clarisonic brush launched in 2004 and was later known as the Mia 1; the Mia 2 with two speeds followed in 2012, a black model marketed toward men, the Alpha Fit, in 2015, and the compact Mia Fit in 2016.[4] L'Oreal acquired the company in 2011, Clarisonic devices made up 14% of the skin care device market in 2018, and L'Oreal announced the brand's discontinuation in July 2020, with Wikipedia noting speculation that cheaper competitors contributed.[4]

The evidence relates to removal of debris and to acne-prone skin during a cleansing regimen. The pollution-model study was designed specifically to compare the brush with manual cleansing against oily particulate soiling [2]. A multi-center cohort study evaluated twice-daily cleansing with an oscillating brush, an acne brush head and a gel cleanser for four weeks in people with mild-to-moderate acne and acne-prone skin [3]. Such a cohort design lacks a control group, so the contribution of the brush separate from the cleanser cannot be determined from it alone.
The device is a cleansing tool and the studies do not address anti-aging outcomes.
A 2019 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology summarised the literature on facial cleansing with a sonic brush and the current recommendations for its use [1].
A 2017 study using an artificial sebum, oil and particulate pollution model assessed cleansing efficacy of a sonic brush versus manual cleansing on human skin [2].

A 2019 multi-center cohort study in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology evaluated four weeks of twice-daily cleansing with an oscillatory sonic brush, an acne brush head and a cleansing gel in people with mild-to-moderate acne and acne-prone skin [3]. Within-study details beyond the design were not available for this article.

Commonly cited concerns are irritation or over-exfoliation with frequent use, rough settings or sensitive and acne-prone skin, and bacterial build-up on bristle heads that are not replaced regularly. Manufacturers generally recommend replacing heads on a schedule and cleaning them between uses; recommendations differ between brands.
Models and heads vary by bristle softness, waterproofing, number of speeds and availability and price of replacement heads, with devices listed at roughly $30 to $200.

angle.text: The brush is used to cleanse the face more thoroughly than hands alone, which users and manufacturers associate with clearer, smoother-looking skin and, in the acne-head cohort study, with cleansing in people with acne-prone skin. The effect applies while the routine is kept up.
